Mariner
MAIR-i-ner
noun
From the Old French marinier, from the Latin marinus, “of the sea” (mare, “sea”); hence a seaman, a sailor, a man whose calling and livelihood are upon the water.

Biblical Definition

A mariner is a seaman — the man whose trade is the deep, who handles rope and oar and sail for his bread. Scripture gives him two great appearances. In Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre he is part of the glory of a merchant empire: “the inhabitants of Zidon and Arvad were thy mariners: thy wise men, O Tyrus, that were in thee, were thy pilots” (Eze 27:8). And he is part of her ruin: “thy mariners, and thy pilots… shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin” (Eze 27:27), until “all that handle the oar, the mariners, and all the pilots of the sea, shall come down from their ships, they shall stand upon the land” (Eze 27:29). The men who mastered the water stand at last on the shore with nothing. In Jonah he is a heathen sailor made to see the hand of God: “then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god” (Jon 1:5), and when at last “they took up Jonah, and cast him forth into the sea: and the sea ceased from her raging” (Jon 1:15), those same heathen feared the LORD exceedingly, offered a sacrifice, and made vows (Jon 1:16). The Psalmist explains why the mariner is set before us at all: “they that go down to the sea in ships… these see the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep” (Psa 107:23–24). No man stands nearer the naked power of God than the mariner, and no man is more tempted to credit his own hand for surviving it.

Webster 1828 Definition

A seaman; a sailor; one whose occupation is to navigate ships upon the sea.

expand to see more

MARINER, a seaman or sailor; one whose occupation is to assist in navigating ships.

From the Latin marinus, “of the sea,” from mare, “the sea.”

It names the working seaman, distinguished from the pilot and the shipmaster who direct him.

The AV joins mariners with pilots and calkers in the trade of Tyre (Eze 27:9, 27).

Jonah’s mariners were heathen sailors brought to fear the LORD exceedingly (Jon 1:5, 16).

Key Scripture

Eze 27:8 — "The inhabitants of Zidon and Arvad were thy mariners: thy wise men, O Tyrus, that were in thee, were thy pilots."

Jon 1:15 — "So they took up Jonah, and cast him forth into the sea: and the sea ceased from her raging."

Eze 27:29 — "And all that handle the oar, the mariners, and all the pilots of the sea, shall come down from their ships, they shall stand upon the land;"

Jon 1:5 — "Then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them. But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep."

Modern Corruption

A plain word for the seaman; the live misuse is the old myth of the self-sufficient man who masters the sea and needs no God upon it.

expand to see more

The temptation the word carries is the oldest flattery of the fallen heart: that the sea is a thing man conquers by skill. Tyre believed it. She built her ships of the fir of Senir and her masts of the cedars of Lebanon, hired the wise men of Gebal to calk her seams, filled her decks with the best mariners of the coast, and said in her heart that the deep was hers. Ezekiel answers that the whole company — mariners, pilots, calkers, men of war — goes down together in the day of her ruin. The modern version of the boast is not a merchant fleet but a technology: charts, engines, satellites, and the settled assumption that the sea has been solved. It has not been solved. The mariner sees the works of the LORD in the deep precisely because the deep will not be tamed, and every seaman who has felt a hull shudder under him knows it whatever he says on shore.

The mercy in the word is that God takes heathen mariners and makes them worshippers. Jonah’s sailors began the chapter each crying to his own god and casting the cargo overboard; they ended it fearing the LORD exceedingly, offering a sacrifice, and making vows — converted in a storm raised by the disobedience of a prophet who slept through it. That is how sovereign grace works: the LORD sends a tempest to chasten one man and gathers a shipload of Gentiles in the doing of it. The mariner is therefore not merely a figure of peril but a standing witness that no man is out of God’s reach on the widest water, and that the LORD who commands the stormy wind commands the hearts of the men He drives with it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means a seaman — a man of the sea, from the Latin for “the sea.”

expand to see more

Mariner — Old French marinier, from Latin marinus, “of the sea.”

The root is mare, “the sea” — the same root behind marine and maritime.

In the AV he is the working seaman, ranked beside pilots and calkers (Eze 27:27).

Ezekiel drowns the whole company with the city they served (Eze 27:27, 29).

Jonah’s mariners are heathen sailors converted in the storm (Jon 1:5, 16).

Usage

"The mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god — and ended the chapter fearing the LORD."

"A mariner sees the works of the LORD in the deep because the deep will not be mastered."

"Tyre’s mariners went down with her merchandise: skill cannot outlive the judgment of God."
